“Moreover, the person who is bound by a contract is trusted, since trust alone is what binds contracts together; but those who are being led to punishment, whether death or some lesser penalty, are put in chains or guarded by officers.”
Ubi vero vel alteri vel utrique creditur, ibi is cui creditur, promittit se praestiturum postea, appellaturque hujusmodi promissum pacti.
“But where one party or both are trusted, the person who is trusted promises to perform later, and this kind of promise is called a contract.”

Rhyme is to verse … — “La rime dans le vers, c’est la couleur dans la peinture.” — “Rhyme in verse is what color is in painting.” Ernest Hello, Le siècle. Les hommes et les idées, Paris 1928, pp. 366–367.
Max Picard — (1888–1965), Swiss philosopher of culture.

Raum is the same word as Rom — See C. Schmitt, “Raum und Rom. Zur Phonetik des Wortes Raum,” in Universitas (1951), pp. 963–967; also in SGN, pp. 491–495. See Nicolaus Sombart, Jugend in Berlin, 6th ed., Frankfurt am Main 2001, p. 252.
fallen for a Caliban — This refers to Gerhard Nebel; see below, notes to pp. 269 and 283.
“Come to the bar with the green orchid …” — A parody of Gottfried Benn’s poem “Allerseelen,” which begins:
Put the fragrant mignonette on the table, bring out the last red asters, and let us speak once more of love, as we did that May.
If you gave an answer, it would be deception — Correctly: “If you gave an answer, you would be deception.”
From Oskar Loerke’s poem “An meinen Dämon,” which Wilhelm Lehmann described as his “favorite poem” by Loerke; see W. Lehmann, Gesammelte Werke in acht Bänden, vol. 7, Stuttgart 2009, pp. 45–46.

Julius Bab — (1880–1955), writer, dramaturge, and theater critic. Bab was one of Schmitt’s early acquaintances; see Tb 1912–15. A letter from Schmitt to Bab dated 13 September 1914 was published by Piet Tommissen in Complexio Oppositorum. Über Carl Schmitt, ed. H. Quaritsch, Berlin 1988, pp. 92–94.
If I cease to act, I am destroyed — F. Schiller, Wallenstein, Act 1, Scene 7:

Show me a way out of this pressure, helpful powers! Show me one that I am capable of taking—I cannot, like some hero of words, some prattler about virtue, warm myself with my own will and thoughts— I cannot proudly say to happiness when it turns its back on me: Go! I do not need you. If I cease to act, I am destroyed.
In the piercing awareness of my nothingness — F. Schiller, Don Carlos, Act 2, Scene 5:
Carlos: …Oh, I do not doubt that we shall soon hear of your victories. You will know how to prove yourself worthy of our gracious trust.
Alba, pointedly: Shall I indeed— in the piercing awareness of my nothingness?

Fons turbatus pede & vena corrupta, est iustus cadens coram impio — Bacon is quoting the Vulgate, Proverbs 25:26: “Like a spring muddied by the foot and a corrupted fountain is the righteous man who gives way before the wicked.”
The Explicatio Bacon gives of this parable —

Praecipit Parabola, rebuspublicis ante omnia cavendum esse de iniquo et infami judicio, in causa aliqua celebri et gravi; praesertim ubi non absolvitur innoxius, sed condemnatur insons. Etenim injuriae inter privatos grassantes turbant quidem et polluunt latices justitiae, sed tanquam in rivulis: verum judicia iniqua, qualia diximus, a quibus exempla petuntur, fontes ipsos justitiae inficiunt et inquinant. Postquam enim tribunal cesserit in partes injustitiae, status rerum vertitur tanquam in latrocinium publicum: fitque plane, ut homo homini sit lupus.

“The parable teaches that, in public affairs, the greatest care must be taken to avoid an unjust and disgraceful judgment in any important and prominent case—especially when the innocent person is not acquitted but is instead condemned.

For injustices committed between private individuals certainly muddy and pollute the waters of justice, but only, so to speak, in the smaller streams. Unjust judgments of the kind we are discussing, however—judgments that become precedents—poison and pollute the very sources of justice themselves.
Once a court has gone over to the side of injustice, the whole condition of affairs changes into something like public robbery, and it becomes plainly true that man is a wolf to man.”
Francis Bacon, The Works of F. Bacon, ed. James Spedding, Robert Leslie Ellis, and Douglas Denon Heath, vol. 3, Boston 1862, pp. 79–80. See also Blumenberg, pp. 185–187.

What can happen to me … — From Friedrich Schnack’s poem “Licht der Welt.” Schmitt owned several of Schnack’s books. The source here is F. Schnack, Das kommende Reich. Gedichte, Hellerau 1920, pp. 104–105.
Who can harm me, from all those evil hosts, when I am allowed to preserve You, tender, ancient spirit of flame?
I have been placed amid the enmity of enemies, amid the anger of cities, amid the breath of hatred from mouths. But I have lit the solemn lamp within me,
in the middle of the midnight hour: sweet light of the world.
He is a Mal-Mann — French mal = bad, evil. A play on the name of Walter Mallmann (1908–1982), an editor at Mohr in Tübingen; see BW Forsthoff (index).

Hegel, Phenomenology, p. 356 — Schmitt quotes from the following edition: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, Phänomenologie des Geistes (= Sämtliche Werke. Krit. Gesamtausgabe der Werke Hegels in zwölf Bänden, ed. and introduced by Otto Weiß), Leipzig 1909. Schmitt’s annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 24638.
In the Suhrkamp edition the passage reads:

“The dead man whose right has been violated knows how to find instruments for his revenge that possess the same reality and force as the power that injured him. These powers are other communities, whose altars have been defiled by dogs or birds carrying the corpse that was denied its proper return to the elemental individual and therefore was not raised into unconscious universality, but remained above ground in the realm of actuality. As the power of divine law it now acquires a self-conscious and actual universality. These communities rise up as enemies and destroy the community that dishonored and shattered its own strength: the piety of the family.”
Hegel, Werke, ed. Eva Moldenhauer and Karl Markus Michel, vol. 3, Frankfurt am Main 1970, pp. 351–352.
See also the entries for 2 July 1948, 15 June 1951, and 2 July 1951.
The ashes will not let go … — See above, note to p. 93.
access to the summit of power — See Carl Schmitt, Gespräch über die Macht und den Zugang zum Machthaber, Pfullingen 1954 and later editions.

Le secret de l’Église catholique — In Villiers de l’Isle-Adam’s novella “L’enjeu” (see above, note to p. 69), an abbé, having lost all his money gambling, stakes the “secret of the Church.” When he loses again and is asked to reveal the secret, he says:
“hélas! le grand secret de l’Église: Il n’y a pas de purgatoire”
“Alas! The great secret of the Church: there is no purgatory.”

Andersch — Alfred Andersch (1914–1980), writer and head of the evening studio at Hessischer Rundfunk, where he also introduced Carl Schmitt. Schmitt’s papers contain seven letters and one postcard from Andersch dating from 1951 to 1954; RW 265 nos. 389–396.

On Hannah Arendt … — Refers to H. Arendt, Elemente und Ursprünge totaler Herrschaft, Munich/Zurich 1986, pp. 108 ff., chapter “The Jews and Society.” This section also quotes Goethe’s review, mentioned below, of Gedichte von einem polnischen Juden, pp. 113–114.
Schmitt used the English edition, The Burden of Our Time, London 1951; his copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 22551.

Poems by a Polish Jew … — Isaschar Falkensohn Behr, Gedichte von einem polnischen Juden, Mitau/Leipzig 1772. This was the first collection of poetry by a German-language Jewish poet. See the modern edition by Andreas Wittbrodt, Göttingen 2002.
Goethe’s review can be found in J. W. Goethe, Gedenkausgabe der Werke, Briefe und Gespräche, ed. Ernst Beutler, 2nd ed., vol. 14, Zurich 1964, pp. 157–160; the quotations are on pp. 158 and 159.

Christianity is Judaism for the people — The sentence repeatedly quoted by Schmitt, “Christianity is Judaism for the multitude, but still it is Judaism,” appears in Benjamin Disraeli’s novel Tancred or the New Crusade.

Schmitt read the book in the abridged German translation by Julius Elbau, published in 1936 by the Jüdische Buchvereinigung Berlin. On p. 281 the line reads: “Christianity is Judaism for the general public.”
For Schmitt, this was the “key sentence” of the book. See Nicolaus Sombart, Jugend in Berlin, 6th ed., Frankfurt am Main 2001, pp. 260 ff.

Thomas Mann says: Christianity is the most beautiful flower of Judaism — “Say what you like: Christianity, this flower of Judaism, remains one of the two basic pillars on which Western civilization rests; the other is Mediterranean antiquity.”
Thomas Mann, Gesammelte Werke, vol. 9, 2nd revised ed., Frankfurt am Main 1974, p. 461.
Goethe says in 1824 — Not in the edition by Hesse cited there, but in J. W. Goethe, Sämtliche Werke nach Epochen seines Schaffens (Munich edition), vol. 13/1, Munich 1992, p. 403.
Stahl-Jolson as early as 1840 — Refers to Friedrich Julius Stahl, Die Kirchenverfassung nach Lehre und Recht der Protestanten, Erlangen 1840.
sbirreria — Refers to the work of the sbirri, judicial and police officers in the Papal States who were militarily organized and armed.

Schmitt quotes from the following edition: Francis Bacon, Fr. Baconi De Verulamio Sermones fideles, Ethici, Politici, Œconomici: Sive Interiora Rerum. Accedunt Faber Fortunæ Colores Boni Et Mali …, Leiden 1644. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 23412.
The passage is not actually on p. 246, but on p. 240:

Cardinales Romani, (qui Theologi sunt, & Fratres & Scholastici,) verbum usurpant, extremi contemptus & convitii, erga negotia Civilia: Vocant enim negotia Civilia, (velut, Belli, Legationum, Iudiciorum, & hujusmodi,) Hispanico vocabulo, Sbirrarias; quod sonat, Munera Lictorum & Scribarum.

“The Roman cardinals, who are theologians, friars, and scholars, use a term of extreme contempt and disdain for civil affairs. They call such matters—war, diplomacy, judicial affairs, and the like—by the Spanish expression sbirreria, meaning work fit for bailiffs and clerks.”

Otto Weininger claims … — Schmitt quotes from his copy of the following edition, inscribed “Carl Schmitt, Düsseldorf, May 1912”: Otto Weininger, Über die letzten Dinge, with a biographical foreword by Moritz Rappaport, 3rd ed., identical to the 2nd, Vienna et al. 1912, pp. 83 ff.
draft of a project — See BW Mohler, p. 105.
If the religious laws of the Roman emperors … — Correctly: “Without the imperial legislation from Constantine through Theodosius, the Greco-Roman religion would still be alive today.”
Jacob Burckhardt, Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen (Kröner Taschenausgabe, 55), Stuttgart 1978, p. 57.
“Blind morsel arches without coarseness …” — R. M. Rilke, poem “Vasen-Bild (Toten-Mahl).” In: idem, Späte Gedichte, Leipzig 1934, p. 128. See Schmittiana VI, 1998, pp. 293–94; BW Mohler, pp. 104–5.
“Everything here will find …” — Quotation from the poem “Die kleine Schöpfung” by Konrad Weiß. In: Weiß, p. 384:

The farmer came home with his hand, stopped and properly took his stand before our three travelers there, and asked: Child, companion, where are you from, where are you going, where is your home? The rooster said: All this will find its place within, and speak from the mind.

“The magnificent sentences in the Phenomenology of Spirit” — In the Moldenhauer and Michel edition of Hegel’s works, Frankfurt am Main 1970, the quotations can be found in vol. 3, pp. 365, 138, and 144.
“The subject-object steamroller rolls …” — See also Schmitt’s ballad “Die Sub-stanz und das Sub-jekt.” In: Civis, 9 June 1955, pp. 29–30; now also in: Gedichte, pp. 16–21.
“Let them mock us, so long as they spare us their pity.” — Walter Warnach, Die Welt des Schmerzes, Pfullingen 1952, p. 111.
amor amaritudinis — “love of bitterness.” Used here as the opposite of amor fati, love of one’s necessary fate, in which Nietzsche saw human greatness.
Peripsema — “scum”; see above, note to p. 23.
Congrua — the minimum income guaranteed to a clergyman from the revenues of his benefice.

“The terror no one dares to name” — See C. Schmitt, “Gesang des Sechzigjährigen.” In: ECS, pp. 92–93; now in: Gedichte, pp. 5–7. Schmitt explains what he meant by this terror in the entry for 7 October 1951.

“A work by Montlosier” — François Dominique de Reynaud de Montlosier (1755–1835), French politician and opponent of ultramontanism. The work quoted was published not in 1826 but in 1827: F. D. de R. de Montlosier, Les Jésuites, les Congrégations et Le parti prêtre en 1827. Mémoire a M. le comte de Villèle …, Paris 1827, p. 65:

“I am well aware that there is a large class of people who do not want anyone concerning themselves with priests. For such people, religion is of no importance, and priests are of no more importance than religion. Their doctrine is this: criticize nothing the priests do, and believe nothing they say.”
